query: How does he compare to Alexander the Great as a general?
answer:
Both men are almost always ranked among history's greatest commanders. On the battlefield alone, Alexander has the cleaner record, while Napoleon fought far more and against tougher odds. Alexander was never defeated in battle. His best-known victories were Granicus, Issus, Gaugamela and the Hydaspes, and in about 13 years he conquered an empire running from Greece to northwestern India before dying at 32 [1]. By one count he fought about forty battles, combats and sieges without a loss [2].

Napoleon fought many more major battles against large coalitions of well-organized European armies. One statistical study counts 43 battles, with 38 wins and 5 losses, including Waterloo. That study, which scores each general against what an average commander would likely have done with the same troops, ranked Napoleon first of all time. Alexander came 10th, mostly because his career was short, not because he was less skilled [3]. It measures battlefield tactics only, not overall strategy.

The usual verdict is that Alexander was the unbeaten conqueror who led from the front. Napoleon is seen as the better organizer and the stronger strategist across whole campaigns. But his conquests fell apart, first in Russia and then at Waterloo. Napoleon admired Alexander and listed him among the seven great commanders every soldier should study. He praised his campaigns as "profoundly calculated, boldly executed and prudently managed," though he also once said Alexander made "no fine maneuvers worthy of a great general" [2]. Which one comes out on top depends on whether you value a perfect record or a longer record against harder opponents.
